The effects and underlying mechanisms of composting and extrusion 
pretreatment on anaerobic biogas production from wheat straw
Guangyin Chen 
a,b, Ya-Ge Lia, Guang-Cai Gea, Yu-Juan Suna and Yu-Xin Zhanga
aSchool of Ecology and Environment, Anhui Normal University, Wuhu, People’s Republic of China; bAnhui Engineering Laboratory of Soil and 
Water Pollution Control and Remediation, Wuhu, People’s Republic of China
ABSTRACT  
The effects of moisture + extrusion and composting + extrusion treatments on the production of 
biogas from the anaerobic digestion (AD) of wheat straw (WS) were systematically investigated. 
The results showed that when the moisture content of WS was adjusted to 55% before 
extrusion and maintained for 24 h, the biogas production of both the unextruded and extruded 
samples reached the highest levels, which were 130.48 and 158.41 mL/g, respectively. Based on 
these results, the WS was further aerobically composted after adjusting its moisture content to 
55%, and then extruded for biogas production. The biogas production of unextruded WS 
initially increased and then decreased, reaching the maximum of 129.40 mL/g when the 
composting temperature rose to 55°C. In contrast, the biogas production of extruded WS 
increased at all composting temperatures and reached the maximum of 150.83 mL/g at 55°C, 
which is 19.49% higher than the initial biogas production of extruded WS at the start of 
composting. Mechanistic analyses indicated that extrusion reduced particle size, increased 
specific surface area, and disrupted lignocellulosic structure, while composting promoted partial 
degradation of hemicellulose and lignin. These structural modifications enhanced substrate 
accessibility and microbial degradation, thereby boosting biogas production. In conclusion, the 
combination of composting and extrusion pretreatment can significantly improve the biogas 
production performance of anaerobic digestion of WS, with an increase ranging from 20.76% to 
43.45%, which is worthy of further research.

KEYWORDS  
Composting pretreatment; 
extrusion pretreatment; 
biogas; wheat straw; 
anaerobic digestion
1. Introduction
In recent years, there has been a growing focus on the 
environmental pollution caused by agricultural waste. 
China produces approximately 900 million tons of crop 
straw annually [1]. Rice straw, maize stalks, and wheat 
straw constitute the primary categories of straw, 
accounting for about 90% of the global total [2]. The 
treatment, recovery, and resource utilization of straw 
remain 
pressing 
challenges 
in 
environmental 
management.
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a biological process in 
which organic substances are decomposed by a consor­
tium of microorganisms working synergistically. Briefly, 
AD consists of four stages: hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acet­
ogenesis, and methanogenesis [3]. AD treatment of 
straw has been adopted in many countries, and AD tech­
nologies for straw are well-developed in developed 
countries. For example, in Europe, biogas production 
from energy crops constitutes a significant portion 
(30–40% wet weight basis of total mixed feed) in agricul­
tural biogas plants [4]. In contrast, the application of AD 
technology for straw in China is still in the developmen­
tal stage.
Although AD is an effective approach to straw treat­
ment, direct AD has limitations regarding the degra­
dation efficiency of raw straw and biogas production

performance. Low gas yields and prolonged digestion 
cycles are major challenges associated with direct AD 
of straw. This is primarily due to the difficulty in degrad­
ing lignocellulosic fibres present in the straw and the 
diminished availability of low molecular weight soluble 
compounds to anaerobic microorganisms [5].
Current pretreatment methods for lignocellulosic 
materials such as straw primarily include physical 
methods, chemical methods, and biological methods. 
Composting is a form of biological pretreatment that 
involves the conversion of organic materials such as 
straw, agricultural by-products, digestate, and animal 
manure into a more decomposed product. Composting 
significantly enhances the quality of the final compost 
products through various decomposition processes [6]. 
However, there is an ongoing debate regarding straw 
composting as a method for straw pretreatment. 
Studies by Yu et al. [7] and Andersen et al. [8] have 
shown that composting-pretreated straw can increase 
the production of biogas. Conversely, research by Gao 
et al. [9], Ajmal et al. [10], and Chen et al. [11] suggests 
that composting does not significantly improve gas pro­
duction from straw. Numerous factors influence the 
efficiency and outcome of composting, including feed­
stock, temperature, carbon-to-nitrogen (C/N) ratio, and 
the moisture content. Research indicates that initial 
moisture content exerts the most significant influence 
on compost maturation. Maintaining a moisture 
content of 60% in the compost mixture is optimal for 
microbial activity [12, 13]. To maintain the moisture 
content 
within 
the 
optimal 
range 
of 
50–65% 
(wet alkaline), water can be added during compost 
turning, and the containers should be covered with 
lids to retain moisture and prevent excessive heat loss 
[14, 15].
The moisture content of straw affects the subsequent 
pretreatment and fermentation processes. Yuan et al. 
[16] demonstrated that a 70% moisture content and 
4% ammonia concentration in straw led to a significant 
increase of 28.55% in biogas yield compared to the 
control treatment. Li et al. [17] investigated the 
impacts of moisture content and additives on H2 pro­
duction, emphasizing that moisture content was the 
most significant factor. Wang et al. [18], in their study 
on composting technology in which deer manure was 
combined with straw, determined an initial moisture 
content of 55%, an initial C/N ratio of 30:1, and a straw 
particle size of 1.5–3.5 cm as the optimal operational 
conditions. Their findings indicated that the initial moist­
ure content had the greatest impact on compost matur­
ity. Currently, there is no report concerning the effects of 
straw composting pretreatment + extrusion on the 
anaerobic fermentation to produce biogas.
While both composting and extrusion have shown 
potential in enhancing the AD of straw individually, 
their mechanisms and effects differ. Composting offers 
a biological degradation route, while extrusion provides 
a rapid physical disruption. Currently, there is a lack of 
systematic research investigating the sequential appli­
cation of composting followed by extrusion as a com­
bined pretreatment strategy for wheat straw. The 
potential synergistic effects of this combination on the 
physicochemical structure of straw and the ultimate 
biogas yield remain unexplored.
This study aims to evaluate the effects of different 
moisture contents on wheat straw, providing critical 
data for subsequent pretreatment and anaerobic diges­
tion; it further systematically assesses the individual and 
combined effects of composting treatment and extru­
sion pretreatment on biogas yield from wheat straw, 
while investigating their impacts on the physicochem­
ical properties of the straw and anaerobic digestion 
efficiency, thereby filling this knowledge gap. The 
specific objectives are: (1) to determine the optimal 
moisture content for wheat straw prior to extrusion pre­
treatment; (2) to assess the impact of composting temp­
erature on the composition and methane potential of 
straw; and (3) to elucidate the synergistic effects of the 
combined pretreatment on straw structure and its sub­
sequent 
enhancement 
of 
anaerobic 
digestion 
performance.
2. Materials and Methods
2.1. Feedstock and Inoculum
The wheat straw (WS) was taken from Funan County, 
Anhui Province, China. The WS was dry and chopped 
manually to a size of about 5cm–10 cm, then set aside 
in a dry and cool place. The total solids (TS), volatile 
solids (VS) and pH of WS were 93.45 ± 0.58%, 89.03 ±  
0.47% and 7.68 ± 0.12, respectively. The inoculum was 
collected from the AD pool at Anhui Linhai Ecology 
Co. and transported to the laboratory, where it was 
mixed with the inoculum in the laboratory for 1 week 
at 37°C before use. The TS, VS, and pH values of the 
inoculum were 4.64 ± 0.08%, 3.36 ± 0.01%, and 7.50 ±  
0.03, respectively.
2.2. Experimental design
The experiments investigated the effect of WS at 
different moisture contents on biogas production after 
extrusion, and also evaluated the use of WS for 
compost pretreatment and extruding the composted 
WS for biogas production based on the determined

G. CHEN ET AL.

optimal moisture content. The experimental treatments 
included the adjustment of the straw moisture content, 
compost pretreatment, straw extrusion pretreatment, 
and anaerobic digestion for biogas production.
2.2.1. Adjustment of the straw moisture content
WS moisture content was adjusted in 48 L plastic con­
tainers. A given amount of wheat straw and an appropri­
ate amount of water were added to the containers to 
adjust the moisture content of the wheat straw to the 
treatment value. The moisture content of the wheat 
straw was adjusted to 20, 40, 55, 70, and 85%. The con­
tainers were covered with lids and left to stand for 24 h. 
One portion of the WS was then sampled for subsequent 
extrusion experiments, and the other portion was placed 
in a plastic bag for the anaerobic digestion experiments.
2.2.2. Compost pretreatment
The composting experiment was carried out at the seed­
ling collection site of Anhui Linhai Ecological Technology 
Co., Ltd. The moisture content of the wheat straw was 
measured before composting. Mix 180 kilograms of 
crushed wheat straw (dry matter mass) with tap water 
to adjust the moisture content to the optimal level 
determined by previous experiments. In those exper­
iments, we evaluated the anaerobic digestion perform­
ance of wheat straw under various moisture conditions 
and identified the optimal moisture level that maximizes 
microbial activity and promotes efficient anaerobic fer­
mentation and methane production. After thorough 
mixing, the straw was piled into 2 × 2 × 1 m stacks, and 
the temperature was recorded every hour for the first 
10 h, then every 12 h after the stack temperature 
reached 55°C. Samples (straw in the red plastic net bag 
at the center of the pile) were taken at the starting 
point of the reactor temperature, at 30, 40, 50, and 55° 
C and above for 2 days, with a sample size of 1 plastic 
box (48 litres). The extracted straw was levelled and 
cooled before being placed in the plastic box. The pH 
values of the straw samples were measured in the 
company laboratory, and samples were stored at −18° 
C in a freezer. The compost samples were analyzed for 
TS, VS, total organic carbon (TOC), total nitrogen (TN), 
cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, with small amounts 
used for FTIR, electron microscopy, and XRD analyses 
and measurements of specific surface area. Before com­
posting, 10 mesh bags were filled with straw of known 
dry matter mass with the previously obtained optimal 
moisture content. The mesh bags were inserted into 
the middle of the compost piles, and two mesh bags 
were removed during each sampling period to deter­
mine the loss rate of total solids.
2.2.3. Extruding treatment
The extrusion process was conducted at Linhai Ecologi­
cal Technology Co., Ltd., located in Funan County, Anhui 
Province, China. The experimental extrusion equipment 
was described in detail by Chen et al. [19]. A twin-screw 
extruder with two counter-rotating screws (TSP180, 
Jinwo Machinery Co., Ltd. Nanjing, China) was used for 
the experiment. The twin-screw extruder utilizes two 
parallel, meshed, and co-rotating modular screws and 
specially structured screw elements to dynamically 
squeeze the fibre materials while conveying them and 
to complete fibre crushing and dissociation by kneading 
between fibres under high concentration and pressure. 
The power supply voltage of the twin-screw extruder 
was 380 V, the frequency was 50 Hz, and the maximum 
power used was 151 kW. The main technical parameters 
included a screw diameter of 180 mm, a screw speed of 
450 r/min, and a screw center distance of 158 mm. 
Untreated, moisture-adjusted, and compost-pretreated 
WS samples were continuously fed into the barrel 
through the inlet orifice by transport screws, and the 
accumulated WS samples were compressed in the 
space between the transport screws and the reversed 
screw element. All extruded WS was collected, placed 
in airtight plastic bags, and stored at 4°C for the analysis 
of physicochemical properties and anaerobic digestion 
experiments. Samples of raw WS and extruded WS 
were collected and dried at 60°C for 3 days. Part of the 
sampled straw was used for SEM and SSA determi­
nations, while another part was crushed and passed 
through a 100-mesh sieve for FTIR and XRD analyses.
2.2.4. Anaerobic digestion
Samples involved in this study included the following 
categories: untreated straw, straw with different moist­
ure contents, straw with different moisture contents 
after extruding, samples of straw compost at different 
temperatures, and samples of straw compost at 
different temperatures after extruding. All these 
samples were used for subsequent analyses, including 
physicochemical property determination and anaerobic 
digestion experiments.
The anaerobic digestion (AD) experiments were 
based on existing literature studies [19]. The AD exper­
iments were performed in triplicate using sequencing 
batch model with a total volume of 1000 mL, while the 
active volume of the reactor was 800 mL. First, 48 g of 
wheat straw (based on dry mass), 500 g of inoculum, 
and distilled water were added to the bioreactor to 
achieve an initial TS loading rate of 6.0% for WS. The bio­
reactor was then flushed with nitrogen (99.9%) for 3 min, 
immediately sealed with a rubber stopper, and

subsequently incubated at (37 ± 1)°C to produce biogas. 
A gas outlet was installed at the top of the bioreactor, 
through which the generated biogas was collected 
into a gas collection cylinder. Meanwhile, two blank bio­
reactors consisting of inoculum and distilled water were 
incubated under the same temperature conditions to 
quantify the background biogas production, and the 
values were subtracted from the total gas production. 
The experiment lasted for 41 days and was terminated 
when no significant biogas production was observed 
for 1 consecutive week. To prevent material stratification 
and excessive floating, each reactor was manually agi­
tated twice daily.
The wheat straw with moisture contents of 30, 40, 55, 
70, and 85%, as well as the above wheat straw after 
extrusion, are referred to as pre- and post-extrusion 
wheat straw, comprising the natural state of straw and 
the extruded straw. The anaerobic digestion exper­
iments were conducted by inoculating each straw treat­
ment separately, and the biogas production data were 
collected for analysis. The uncomposted, composted, 
and extruded compost samples were inoculated for 
the anaerobic digestion experiments. The wheat straws 
that reached ambient temperatures, 30, 40, 50, and 55° 
C and above after 2 days were labelled as T0, T1, T2, 
T3, T4, and T5. The wheat straw that reached ambient 
temperature, 30, 40, 50, and 55°C and above after 2 
days was labelled as L0, L1, L2, L3, L4, and L5 after 
being extruded and composted. Samples were collected 
on days 0, 2, 5, 9, 16, 25, and 41 of the anaerobic diges­
tion experiment using compost extruded materials, and 
the pH, electrical conductivity (EC), total volatile fatty 
acids (TVFAs), soluble chemical oxygen demand 
(SCOD), and alkalinity of the fermentation broth were 
determined. After the experiment, the solid samples 
were filtered through a coarse cotton cloth, and the 
TS, VS, and ash content were measured and used to cal­
culate the total solid (TS) loss of the fermented straw. 
After drying and crushing a portion of the solid sample 
through a 100-mesh screen, the sample was used for 
Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), X-ray 
diffraction (XRD), and scanning electron microscopy 
(SEM) analyses.
2.3. Analytical methods
A mercury thermometer was placed at the center part of 
the composting pile to monitor the core temperature, 
and three additional mercury thermometers were used 
to measure the temperature at three different central 
points of the pile. The determination of total solids (TS) 
was carried out by drying the sample at 105°C for 24 h 
to a constant weight using the differential weight 
method. The volatile solids (VS) were determined by 
igniting the dried sample at 550°C for 4 h in a muffle 
furnace, and the difference in weight before and after 
ignition was calculated as the VS. The pH value of the 
dry WS samples was determined by preparing an 
aqueous slurry. Approximately 10 g of the dry WS 
sample was mixed with 100 mL of distilled water, and 
the mixture was stirred for 30 min. The pH of the slurry 
was then measured using a pH metre (PHB-4, Leici, 
China). Daily biogas production was measured by 
water displacement and recorded daily. The cumulative 
biogas production was calculated as the sum of the daily 
biogas production over the entire experimental period. 
A continuous gas collection method is employed when 
biogas production varies across different stages. For 
instance, during phases of lower biogas production, 
biogas is collected continuously over several days, with 
methane concentration measurements conducted uni­
formly on the final collection day. The collected gas 
was passed into a GC-5890N gas chromatograph for 
measurement. The column used in the gas chromato­
graph was FFAP, and the parameters for measuring 
methane concentration were an inlet B temperature of 
105°C, a detector B temperature of 120°C, b uo a 
column box temperature of 80°C, and a single sample 
measurement time of 5 min (GC5890N, Nanjing Kejie 
Analytical Instrument Co., Ltd, China). The calculation

centration on that day, %; a is the daily biogas concen­

The determination of TVFAs was conducted following

Brunauer–Emmett–Teller specific surface area and por­

Wheat straw was air-dried, crushed, and passed

870FT, Nicolet, USA) and X-ray diffraction (XTRA, 
Thermo Fisher, USA) analysis. Crystallinity was calculated 
following the method described in a previous study [19]. 
The surface structure of wheat straw was observed using 
a scanning electron microscope (Tescan Mira4, Tescan,

wheat straw was observed using a 2 μm scanning elec­

2.4. Mapping and data analysis
One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) (P < 0.05) and 
factor analysis were performed on data from three repli­
cates of each treatment; results were reported as mean 
values ± standard deviation. ANOVA and factor analysis 
were carried out with the software package SPSS 
(Version 21, IBM Inc., 2012). Jade 6.0 was used for XRD 
pattern fitting. Origin 2022 was used for plotting of 
experimental data, and Excel 2019 software was used 
for processing of experimental data.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Effects of wheat straw with different 
moisture contents on AD before and after 
extrusion
Figure 1 shows biogas production from wheat straw at 
various moisture contents, before and after extrusion. 
Extrusion increased biogas production. This improve­
ment is primarily attributed to the reduced particle 
size of the wheat straw after extrusion the treatment 
altered the aggregation state and porosity of the 
wheat straw matrix, promoting an increase in surface 
area and a decrease in crystallinity. This finding is con­
sistent with the results reported in a previous study 
[21]. Minimal changes in biogas production were 
observed at 40% and 85% moisture content, indicating 
that both extremely high and low moisture levels limit 
biogas production. Excessive moisture also increases 
extrusion power consumption [18]. The moisture 
content of composting materials also affects the bioa­
vailability of oxygen in microbial processes.
Water is essential for the decomposition process, and 
moisture stress is one of the most common limiting 
factors for microbial activity on solid organic substrates. 
However, when the moisture content exceeds 65%, air in 
the pore spaces of the raw material is displaced by 
water, resulting in anaerobic conditions, odour issues, 
and reduced decomposition rates [22, 23]. Maintaining 
a moisture content of approximately 60% in the sub­
strate mixture is optimal for microbial activity [6, 12]. 
Among the five treatments, 55% moisture content in 
wheat straw showed the highest biogas production 
after extrusion (158.41 mL·g−1·TS−1), a 21.4% improve­
ment compared to pre-extrusion. Thus, the pre-treat­
ment can enhance biogas production from wheat 
straw, and different moisture contents of the wheat 
straw also exert a significant influence on biogas pro­
duction. The results indicated that wheat straw with a 
moisture content of 55% and extrusion pre-treatment 
exhibited optimal biogas production, providing support­
ing data for subsequent experiments.
3.2. Effects of compost pretreatment on straw
3.2.1. Effect on dry matter loss
The variation in compost pile temperature during the 
composting process is presented in Figure 2a. During 
the first 10 h of the experiment, the compost pile temp­
erature increased rapidly, and reached 55°C at 21 h. By 
29 h, the temperature of the compost pile inside the 
reactor had reached 60°C. At this point, the reactor 
was turned over, leading to a temperature drop to 20° 
C. The purpose of turning over the compost pile was 
to alter the positioning of internal and external wheat 
straw, thereby enhancing biogas exchange between 
the compost pile and its surroundings, improving 
microbial growth conditions, and increasing the degra­
dation rate of organic matter [8]. After turning, the 
compost pile temperature increased rapidly again, stabi­
lizing at approximately 57°C and remaining stable for 
40 h.
According to the experimental design, samples were 
collected at the initiation of the experiment (T0), as well 
as when the pile temperature reached 30°C (T1), 40°C 
(T2), 50°C (T3), 55°C (T4), and when it exceeded 55°C 
for 2 days (T5). Corresponding composting experiments 
were conducted at 0, 11, 14, 18, 21, and 69 h, with the 
remainder used for anaerobic digestion and biogas pro­
duction experiments.

The results of TS loss during WS composting are 
presented in Figure 2b. The composting process 
involves the microbial decomposition and utilization 
of WS organic matter, as well as heating of the WS 
pile. A substantial loss of WS dry matter occurred 
during composting, primarily due to the decompo­
sition of organic matter. WS’s TS loss rate exhibited a 
gradual increase during the initial 21 h of composting, 
and reached 28% by 69 h. The TS loss rate continued 
to increase with higher pile temperature and longer 
duration. 
Higher 
pile 
temperatures 
accelerated 
the decomposition of organic matter, thereby 
resulting in a further significant loss of WS dry 
matter [24]. This study primarily focused on the 
influence of composting pre-treatment on AD, where 
dry matter loss inevitably leads to reduced methane 
production from WS anaerobic digestion. Therefore, 
no additional samples were collected after 69 h of 
composting.
3.2.2. Effect of composting pre-treatment on wheat 
straw AD
The biogas production trends of WS under different 
treatments displayed analogous patterns, with initial 
rapid increases during the early fermentation phase 
(Figure 3a). Days 6–10 corresponded to the peak 
biogas production phase, followed by a sharp decline 
in methane production. By day 25, the daily biogas pro­
duction dropped to below 50 mL and stabilized. Figure 
3b illustrates the total biogas production from raw and 
composted WS under different composting tempera­
tures. All composted WS treatment groups exhibited 
higher methane yields in comparison to raw WS, with 
the group composted at 55°C achieving the highest pro­
duction of 128.00 mL/g. This represented a 21.74% rela­
tive increase in total biogas production in comparison to 
raw straw. The results demonstrate that composting pre­
treatment significantly enhances biogas production 
from wheat straw AD, which is consistent with findings 
reported by Yu et al. [7] and Andersen et al. [8].

3.3. Effect of extrusion pre-treatment on the AD 
of wheat straw
3.3.1. Biogas production
Samples from group T0 were collected before pile for­
mation and heating. At this stage, the wheat straw 
served as the initial substrate for AD experiments follow­
ing mixing pretreatment, and biogas production was 
measured.
The results demonstrated a total biogas production of 
5220.67 mL from the initial WS, and this value increased 
to 6438.33 mL after mixing pretreatment, marking a 
23.32% improvement in biogas production (Table 1). 
These results served as a reference for subsequent 
blank groups. Biogas production from WS subjected to 
different composting temperatures was compared 
before and after mixing pretreatment. The percentage 
improvement in biogas production was detailed in 
Table 1. Apart from the blank group data, mixing pre­
treatment enhanced the AD performance of WS, with 
the improvement in biogas production ranging from 
18% to 39%. The differences in improvement between 
the blank group and other treatment groups were 
minor but consistent. Thus, mixing pretreatment effec­
tively enhances biogas production from the anaerobic 
digestion of WS.
3.3.2. pH values
Research indicates that pH directly regulates the process 
and intermediate products of AD. The optimal pH range 
for this process has been reported to range from 6.8 to 
7.4 [25]. Figure S1 depicts the pH variation in the AD 
system using compost-pretreated and untreated WS 
before mixing. The pH trends among different treatment 
groups exhibited an initial convergence, with the pH 
value first decreasing, then increasing, and finally stabi­
lizing. The pH value decreased continuously from day 
0 to day 5, reaching its minimum on day 5. From day 6 
to day 9, the pH value increased and stabilized there­
after. The post-mixing pH variation exhibited a similar 
trend (Figure S2). This phenomenon was primarily attrib­
uted to the substantial production of organic acids 
during the initial stage of AD, thereby leading to a pH 
decrease in the early stage of the AD reactor. However, 
as the process continued, the production of ammonia 
increased, raising the pH value to 7.0–7.2. Methane pro­
duction stabilizes when the pH reaches 7.2–8.2. Post- 
mixing pH fluctuations exhibited smaller magnitudes 
and greater stability compared to pre-mixing conditions. 
This observation might be attributed to the disruption of 
the WS surface rigid structures after mixing, which facili­
tated the breakdown of WS by fibre-degrading microbial 
communities, thereby lowering the pH value.

3.3.3. VFAs variation
The variation in VFAs during the AD process before and 
after mixing is presented in Figure 4(a) and (b). The 
trends in VFA contents for WS were similar before and 
after mixing, exhibiting an initial increase followed by 
a decrease and subsequent stabilization. During fermen­
tation, the VFA content increased until the 5th day, with 
the highest value observed in wheat straw subjected to 
mixing pretreatment at a composting temperature of 
50°C, which reached 8296.67 mg/L. From day 6 to day 
16, the VFA content decreased gradually and stabilized 
after day 17. However, the magnitude of variation in 
VFA content after mixing was smaller in comparison to 
that before mixing. This could be attributed to the trans­
formation of WS into a softer fibrous material after 
mixing, as the process separates cellulose, hemicellulose, 
and lignin, thereby facilitating more efficient decompo­
sition of organic matter by microbes and promoting 
VFA accumulation.
Under controlled fermentation conditions, VFAs accu­
mulated gradually in the substrate during the initial 
stage of fermentation, primarily dominated by acetic 
acid throughout the fermentation process. This was 
attributed to the rapid growth of acidogenic bacteria 
during the biogas fermentation process, which convert 
substrates into VFAs. The accumulation of VFAs occurred 
because the accumulated VFAs could not be timely con­
verted into methane.
3.4. Effect of composting and extrusion on AD of 
wheat straw
3.4.1. Effect on biogas production
In this study, AD was conducted on WS in the L0, L1, L2, 
L3, L4, and L5 groups, and the biogas production rates of 
WS in these groups were compared. Composting com­
bined with extrusion pretreatment enhanced the 
biogas production from wheat straw. Composting treat­
ment enhanced the biogas production of WS at room 
temperature, 30, 40, 50, and 55°C and above for 2 days 
(Figure 5). The biogas production initially increased 
with increasing composting temperature, attaining a 
maximum value of 6144 mL when the temperature 
reached 55°C. However, when temperatures above 55° 
C were maintained for an additional 2 days, the pro­
duction of biogas decreased to 5598 mL. After compost­
ing 
pre-treatment 
combined 
with 
extrusion 
pretreatment, the biogas production at various com­
posting temperatures increased significantly, exhibiting 
a trend of first increasing and then decreasing. After 
extrusion pretreatment at 55°C, the biogas production 
of WS was 7240 mL, which was 43.45% higher than 
that of the control group. When composting tempera­
tures were further increased and maintained for 2 
days, combined with extruding pretreatment, the 
biogas production of WS decreased to 6460 mL.
To investigate the reasons behind the enhanced AD 
biogas production due to pretreatment, specific 
surface area tests were conducted on WS samples 
from each group. The results (Table 2) indicated that 
composting pretreatment alone did not increase the 
specific surface area of WS. The BET specific surface 
areas of L0 and T4 were 2.6983 and 2.6133 m2/g, respect­
ively. However, when combined with extrusion pretreat­
ment, there was a significant increase in the specific 
surface area of WS, consistent with the experimental 
results of biogas production. The BET specific surface 
area of L4 was 9.9347 m2/g, which indicated a highly sig­
nificant increase. Therefore, one reason for the enhanced 
biogas production from WS treated with combined com­
posting and extrusion pretreatment is the increase in 
specific surface area.

a gradual decreasing trend, with the highest intensity 
observed for original WS and the lowest for the AD 
group. All WS samples exhibited a broad absorption 
band at around 3394 cm−1, which is attributed to the 
O–H stretching vibrations of hydrogen-bonded hydroxyl 
groups, primarily from cellulose. This absorption band 
shifted slightly to a lower wavenumber value of 
3394 cm−1. The absorption band near 2924 cm−1 rep­
resents the C–H stretching vibrations of cellulose [26]. 
The absorption band around 1736cm−1 is assigned to 
the characteristic bending or stretching vibrations of 
functional groups in cellulose [27]. The absorbance 
intensity of hemicellulose at 1045 cm−1 was significantly 
higher for original WS than that for composted at 55°C, 
composted at 55°C with extrusion, and after AD samples. 
The absorbance intensity of hemicellulose at 1045 cm−1 
in the original WS was close to that for the WS treated 
with compost at 55°C with extrusion and after AD, 
although a distinct diagnostic peak for hemicellulose 
was observed at this wavenumber.
The infrared absorption band near 1504 cm−1 is 
assigned to the C = C stretching vibration of aromatic 
rings in lignin [28]. The band near 1240 cm−1 is a diag­
nostic peak for the C–O–C stretching vibration of cellu­
lose [29]. Hemicellulose, a polysaccharide with a 
complex FTIR absorption pattern, exhibits characteristic 
absorption peaks in the range of 1200–1900 cm−1. This 
region primarily involves ring vibrations and overlaps 
with the stretching vibrations of C–OH side groups and 
C–O–C glycosidic bond vibrations. The absorption peak 
at 1045 cm−1 is closely associated with hemicellulose 
[30].
The infrared absorption band intensities of original 
WS were greater than those of the WS composted at 
55°C, composted at 55°C with extrusion, and after AD. 
This indicates a decrease in the hydrogen bonding of 
cellulose and the cleavage of methyl or methylene 
groups, which may contribute to a decrease in WS crys­
tallinity. Additionally, the infrared absorption band 
intensity at 1504 cm−1 was significantly decreased, 
suggesting the cleavage of important ester bonds in 
lignin.
3.4.3. XRD analysis
Pretreatment modifies the crystalline structure and crys­
tallinity of cellulose, thereby affecting cellulose’s enzy­
matic hydrolysis efficiency. Therefore, X-ray diffraction 
(XRD) analysis was employed to assess the crystallinity 
and structure of WS before and after pretreatment. 
Wheat straw samples subjected to composting at 55°C, 
composting at 55°C with extrusion, and after AD exhib­
ited typical cellulose structures (Figure 6b). In the XRD 
patterns, WS samples exhibited a prominent peak at 
26.8° and a minor peak at 22.5°. The positions of these 
peaks did not differ significantly among the various 
treatments, indicating that the crystalline regions of 
WS were not significantly destroyed during the pretreat­
ment and AD processes. Compared to untreated WS, 
minimal changes were observed in crystallinity, peak 
intensity, and grain size following pretreatment and sub­
sequent AD fermentation. Although crystallinity, peak 
intensity, and grain size all increased with WS pretreat­
ment. The crystal plane peaks of WS composted at 55° 
C, composted at 55°C with agitation, composted at 55° 
C with extrusion, and after AD were narrower and

Each treated WS sample exhibited a strong peak at

process, which is consistent with the FTIR results.
4. Conclusion
This study confirmed extrusion pretreatment enhanced 
the biogas production of WS through anaerobic diges­
tion, with the best effect achieved at an initial moist­
ure content of 55%, increasing the gas production by 
21.4% compared to the non-extruded group. Compost­
ing enhanced WS gas production via structural 
destruction, with 55°C as the advisable termination 
temperature, increasing output by 21.74%. Extrusion- 
composting combined pretreatment had a synergistic 
effect. Under the condition of being maintained at 
55°C for 21 h, the gas production of WS was signifi­
cantly increased by 43.45% compared to the control 
group, which was superior to the single pretreatment 
methods. The sequential combined pretreatment of 
composting and extrusion is a high efficiency pretreat­
ment strategy of straw by synergistic biological and 
physical action.
